2027-07-08.title: Thursday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: “Welcome him as you would welcome me”: Paul pleads for Onesimus and takes his debt on his own account
The disciples forget to bring bread: “Do you not remember the five loaves?” Beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees
2027-07-08.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. The Panchangam prints the Epistle as “ഫിലെ 1:17–22”; this is read as the Letter to Philemon, verses 17 to 22, since that letter has a single chapter.
2027-07-08.verse: So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.
theo: The Letter to Philemon is the shortest of St Paul's letters and the most personal. It is a single page written from prison to a friend at Colossae, and its subject is a man named Onesimus, who had been in Philemon's household as a slave and had left it. Somehow Onesimus met Paul, and in that meeting he became a brother in Christ. Paul now sends him back with this letter. Today's verses are the heart of the appeal: “So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.” Paul does not command, though he could. He puts himself in the place of Onesimus: receive him as you would receive me. Then comes the sentence that Christian preachers have loved for two thousand years: “If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand: I will repay it.” In a few words Paul is doing what Christ did for us: he takes the debt of another onto his own account and signs for it with his own hand. The verse that comes just before today's reading says what Paul hopes Philemon will see: Onesimus is returning “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). The Church has never read the letter as an approval of slavery; in time the Gospel it carries has undone it, and the Church teaches that the enslavement of human beings is a grave sin (Catechism 2414).

Paul ends with gentle words that show a whole way of life: “Yes, brother, let me have this benefit from you in the Lord! Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I am writing to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. One thing more: prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping through your prayers to be restored to you.” He trusts Philemon to go beyond what is asked, and he counts on the prayer of the house community, for the prayers of Philemon's family are the means by which Paul hopes to be released and to come to them. A guest room, a prayer and a forgiven debt: this is how the Gospel moves into a home. In Kerala, where a guest is treated as a blessing and a house is judged by the welcome it gives, the letter has a special ring. Welcome him as you would welcome me is a rule for the parish, for the family, and for every household that has to receive someone whom it would prefer not to see.

The Gospel looks at the disciples on the lake shore. They have crossed to the other side and “had forgotten to bring any bread.” The Lord, who has just met the Pharisees and Sadducees demanding a sign (Matthew 16:1–4), says: “Watch out, and beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” The disciples only think of their empty baskets: “It is because we have brought no bread.” Jesus, perceiving this, says: “You of little faith, why are you talking about having no bread? Do you still not perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?” The remedy for worry is memory: to count again what the Lord has already done. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2). Only then does he explain: “He had not told them to beware of the yeast of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Yeast is a small thing that works in secret and spreads through the whole dough: “A little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough” (Galatians 5:9). Jesus names what can spread in a community, pride, hypocrisy, the demand for signs without faith. He is arguing within his own people, as the prophets did, and the warning is for each one of us, not for others. The yeast is not always bad: in the Antiochene tradition of our Church the bread of the Holy Qurbono is leavened, and the Lord himself says that the kingdom is like yeast. What counts is what spreads. Today we ask the Lord to keep the yeast of our hearts good, and to make us remember.
outline: Ask: what debt of another person could I take onto my own account today, and whom could I welcome as I would welcome Paul?

Paul and Onesimus: a brother rather than a slave; the debt written on Paul's own account.
Point 2 · A guest room and a prayer
Trusting the house to do even more; the Gospel enters a home through welcome and prayer.

live: Welcome as you would welcome Christ (Philemon 17)
Receive one person this week whom you would find it easier to avoid, with the same courtesy that you would show to an honoured guest.
Quietly pay or forgive a small debt, in money, time or an old grievance, as if it were charged to your own account.
Each evening this week write down three gifts that the Lord gave you that day, so that worry is answered by memory.
2027-07-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you took our debt onto your own account and paid it with your own hand on the Cross. Teach us to welcome one another as you have welcomed us, and to see in every person a brother or sister for whom you died. Make our homes places of welcome, with a guest room and an open door, and let the prayers of our families be heard. When we worry about our empty baskets, remind us of the loaves you have multiplied, and keep us from the yeast of pride, hypocrisy and little faith. Let the yeast of your kingdom work in us until the whole dough is leavened. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono we are welcomed by Christ as guests at his table, and, as he multiplied the loaves for the five thousand and the seven for the four thousand, he gives us his own Body in abundance: we remember what he has done, and we receive him.

quick: Paul asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus as he would welcome Paul himself, and to charge any debt to Paul's account.
Paul trusts Philemon to do more than he asks, and asks for a guest room and the prayers of the household.
The disciples forget bread; Jesus asks them to remember the loaves and baskets, and warns against the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
2027-07-08.action: Welcome one person warmly today, as if Christ himself were the guest, and quietly forgive or take on one small debt.
2027-07-08.question: Have I forgotten what the Lord has already done for me?

family.explain: St Paul wrote a short letter to his friend Philemon about a man named Onesimus. Onesimus had been a slave in Philemon's house and had gone away, but he had met Paul and become a friend of Jesus. Paul asked Philemon to welcome him back as a brother, and said that if Onesimus owed anything, Paul would pay it. In the Gospel the friends of Jesus are worried because they have forgotten to bring bread. Jesus reminds them how he fed five thousand with five loaves and four thousand with seven loaves. He does not want us to worry; he wants us to remember how kind God has been to us.
family.intention: We pray for families who are worried about money or food, and for those who have to forgive someone.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom can we welcome as a guest this week? What is one good thing God did for us recently?”

illus: A grocer in a small town near Pala kept a ledger for credit sales, the kadam book. A widow who bought rice and lamp oil on credit fell behind through a long illness, and the grocer, who was not an unkind man, had begun to speak sharply about it. The parish priest, who heard of it, said nothing to the widow. On the day his own small pension was paid he went to the shop, asked to see the page, and told the grocer to put the amount on his own account. When the widow came to thank him, he waved his hand and said that he had learnt the trick from a very short letter of St Paul. The grocer, who read the letter that night, said later that it was the first time he had understood why the parish kept a guest room in the presbytery.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you welcomed us and took our debts onto yourself. Teach us to welcome one another, to remember all your gifts and to beware of the yeast that spoils. Amen.
share: Welcome him as you would welcome me (Philemon 17). Whom do I find it hardest to welcome?
Charge that to my account (Philemon 18). What have I been asked to carry for someone, and what has Christ carried for me?
Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand? (Matthew 16:9). Which gifts of God should I recall when I worry?
pm.resp: Lord, make us remember and make us welcome.
interc: For the Church, that she may welcome the stranger, the poor and the returning with the welcome of Christ.
For those who are enslaved or trafficked and for all who work in unjust conditions, that they may be released and be treated as brothers and sisters.
For the families who are worried about their daily bread, that they may remember God's generosity and find help.
For those who must forgive a debt or a wrong, that they may do so from the heart.
For our parish and our families, that the yeast of pride and hypocrisy may be removed, and the yeast of the kingdom may work in us.
pm.close: Father, in your Son you took our debt upon yourself and welcomed us as your own. Teach us to welcome and to forgive, to remember your gifts, and to be leavened by your kingdom. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, the short Letter to Philemon asks a hard thing in a gentle way. Onesimus, who had been a slave in the house of Philemon, is coming back, and Paul says: So if you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me (Philemon 17). Then he says: If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand: I will repay it (Philemon 18–19). This is a picture of Christ, who took our debt on his own account and paid it with his own hand on the Cross. In the verse just before this reading Paul says that Onesimus now comes back no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16).

Paul adds: Confident of your obedience, I am writing to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. And he asks: prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping through your prayers to be restored to you (Philemon 21–22). A welcome, a guest room and a prayer: this is how the Gospel enters a home.

In the Gospel the disciples are crossing the lake, and they have forgotten to bring bread. Jesus warns them of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees, but they think of their empty baskets. He says: You of little faith, why are you talking about having no bread? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? (Matthew 16:8–9). The cure for worry is to remember what the Lord has done. And the yeast he warns of is the teaching of pride and hypocrisy, which a little spreads through the whole dough.
So let us welcome someone whom we find hard to welcome, let us forgive a debt, and let us count again the gifts of God, so that the yeast of his kingdom may work in us. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago a man named Onesimus had gone away from his master's house, and then he became a friend of Jesus. St Paul wrote a letter to the master, Philemon, and asked him to welcome Onesimus back as a brother. Paul even said that he would pay whatever Onesimus owed! That is just what Jesus does for us when we say sorry. In the Gospel the friends of Jesus forgot to take bread and began to worry. Jesus reminded them how he had fed thousands with a few loaves. When you worry, remember how good God has been. And this week, welcome somebody who is new or alone: sit with them and play with them.
